recipe.history:
Broccoli rabe — known in Italian as cime di rapa or rapini — is a leafy green vegetable of the Brassica family with origins in the Mediterranean region, most likely the coastal areas of southern Italy and possibly the eastern Mediterranean. Despite its name and superficial resemblance to broccoli, it is more closely related to turnips, and its culinary character is entirely its own: bitter, assertive, slightly peppery, with small clusters of bud-like florets and thick, tender stems. In southern Italy, and particularly in the regions of Campania, Puglia, and Calabria, broccoli rabe has been a staple of the working-class diet for centuries. It appears in the classic Pugliese dish of orecchiette con cime di rapa — ear-shaped pasta tossed with blanched, sautéed broccoli rabe, garlic, red chili, and olive oil — one of the great peasant dishes of Italy, born from the necessity of making something extraordinary from the bitterest of garden greens. The technique of blanching the broccoli rabe in salted boiling water before sautéing it in olive oil with garlic is ancient, learned, and purposeful: the blanching tames the raw bitterness to something more nuanced and elegant without eliminating it entirely.

Broccoli rabe arrived in the United States primarily through Italian immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Italian immigrant communities in Philadelphia, New York, and New Jersey preserved their culinary traditions faithfully, and broccoli rabe became a fixture of Italian American cooking — most famously in the Philadelphia roast pork sandwich, where the bitter green is paired with sharp provolone to create what many food writers consider the greatest sandwich in America. The leap to burger topping was a short one for any cook who had eaten that sandwich, and the pairing of sautéed broccoli rabe with sharp provolone on a beef patty brings the same logic to bear: the bitterness of the rabe cuts through the fat of the beef with surgical precision, while the sharp, slightly piquant provolone adds a salty, acidic note that ties everything together. It is a burger that rewards those who appreciate complexity and depth over sweetness and comfort.

I first made a broccoli rabe burger after a week of eating roast pork sandwiches in Philadelphia, returning home so thoroughly convinced of the rabe-provolone combination that I wanted to apply it to everything. I blanched a large bunch of broccoli rabe until it was just tender and vibrantly green, squeezed out the water, and sautéed it hard in olive oil with crushed red pepper and more garlic than any reasonable recipe would advise. The kitchen smelled like the best Italian-American diner I have ever been in. I pulled a patty off the cast iron at 132 degrees, placed it on the bun, heaped the garlicky, spicy rabe on top, and laid two slices of sharp provolone over it all so the cheese softened in the heat. My wife said it was the best burger I had made that year. I agreed, though I said it more loudly.

The bitter assertiveness of broccoli rabe needs a medium rare patty the way a bitter aperitivo needs good ice and a twist of orange — the richness of the undercooked beef is not excess but necessary counterweight. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the beef patty offers maximum fat content in liquid form, maximum moisture, and the full, complex Maillard crust that provides the textural and flavor anchor for everything laid on top. The bitter rabe against the fatty, rosy medium rare patty is a counterpoint of flavors that only resolves beautifully because both elements are at their optimal state. Overcook the patty and the balance tips — suddenly the bitter green dominates an increasingly neutral, dry piece of meat, and the whole composition loses its center of gravity.
ingredients: 1 large bunch broccoli rabe (rapini), about 1 lb, tough stems trimmed
12 slices sharp provolone (2 per burger — the sharper the better)
Garlic aioli (2 egg yolks, 1 cup neutral oil, 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp Dijon, 1/2 tsp salt)
Crushed red pepper flakes to finish
instructions: 1. Make the ciabatta-style buns: Combine yeast, warm water, sugar, and olive oil; let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flours and salt; stir until a shaggy, wet dough forms. This dough should be quite sticky — do not add more flour. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3–4 minutes, or use a stand mixer with dough hook on medium for 5 minutes.

2. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let rise at room temperature 1.5–2 hours until doubled and very bubbly. Line a baking sheet with parchment and dust generously with flour. Gently pour dough out and, using floured hands and a bench scraper, fold the dough over itself a few times without deflating. Divide into 6 rough oval portions and place on prepared sheet. Dust tops with flour, cover loosely, and proof 45 minutes.
3. Bake at 450°F for 18–20 minutes until deeply golden and hollow-sounding when tapped. Cool completely on a wire rack.

4. Make the garlic aioli: Whisk 2 egg yolks with Dijon mustard, minced garlic, and a pinch of salt. Whisk in neutral oil drop by drop at first, then in a thin steady stream, until thick and emulsified. Whisk in lemon juice and salt. Adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Blanch the broccoli rabe: Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a boil. Add broccoli rabe and blanch 2–3 minutes until stems are just tender and color is vivid green. Drain and immediately transfer to an ice bath to stop cooking. Drain again and squeeze out excess water firmly. Roughly chop into 2-inch pieces.

6. Sauté the broccoli rabe: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add sliced garlic and cook 60 seconds until golden and fragrant. Add crushed red pepper flakes. Add the blanched, squeezed broccoli rabe and toss to coat in the garlic oil. Season with salt, cook 3–4 minutes until heated through and slightly caramelized in places. Finish with a squeeze of lemon juice. Keep warm.
7. Prepare the patties: Form ground beef into 6 patties (about 4 oz each), 3/4 inch thick with a center dimple. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil. Sear patties dimple-side up 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip, place 2 slices of sharp provolone on each patty, and cook 2–3 more minutes until cheese is melted and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3–4 minutes tented with foil.
9. Toast bun halves cut-side down in a dry skillet or under the broiler 1–2 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread garlic aioli on both bun halves. Place the rested, double-provolone patty on the bottom bun. Heap a generous portion of sautéed broccoli rabe over the patty. Drizzle with a little extra-virgin olive oil. Zest a little lemon over the top, add a pinch of crushed red pepper flakes and flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun and serve immediately.
